MR. BRIGHT AND MR. COBDEN. Iris rather MON than twelve years since the country heard with • sorrow such as the death of e politician rarely evokes, that Richard Cobden had breathed his last. The scene in the House of Commons must have been of the most impressive kind. Leaders of both political parties divided the honour of giving voice to the universal regret at the lose of one whose patentof nobility was made out by no human hand, save, instrumentally, by his own. Hr. Bright said very little. At some calmer moment, when I may have the opportunity of addressing my countrymen, twill endeavour," he observed, to show the lesson that I think may be learned from the life and character of my friend." The " gnawing tooth of time" has 'spared Richard Cobden's memory, and the recriminations of party have fallen harm- , leerily about his good name. For he worked for higher than party ends. This is how it comes to pass that a grateful nation will never, for her own sake, allow his ante to fall into unheeded forgetfulness. The quaint lines of George Herbert convey a truth which mere cleverness is apt to raise—

--- o Outs the &mous of the just Smell sweet, nod blossom trout the dust." There is something both touching and elevating in the thought of a friend- ship begun, continued, and ended in the love of truth and the enthnsimm of humanity; and such • frientiehip was—nay I le—that of Richard Cobden and John Might, No scheme of mutual aggran- disement knit these twain together ; it was • partnership that sprang out of a holy anguish on one side, and a wise sympathy on the other. Let the survivor describe its origin; the simple beauty of his words can 'lose do justice to it.-- I was in Leamington, and Mr. Cobden called on me. I was then in the depths of grief, I may almost say of despair, for the light and sunshine of my house had been extinguished All that was left on earth of my ,yousg wife, except the memory of • sainted hte and a too brief happiness, was lying still and cold in the chamber above us. Mr. Cobden called upon me as my friend, and addressed me, as you may suppose, with word of condolence. After a time, he looked up and said; There are thousands and tens of thousands of homes in England at this moment whom wives and mothers are dying of hunger. Now, when the first paroxysm of great grief is poet, 1 would advise you to come to me, and we will never rest until the Corn Laws are repealed.'" What a Moon is here for the selfishly sorrowful ! History records and fictions shadow forth many a " marriage of true minds," but nobler con- secration for rrivate grief than a lifelong devotion to the public good, who has seen or can hope to .e 0 And, onCobden's part, what happy intuition and vigilant readiness to "take occasion by the hand—at once easing the burden of individual heart. trouble, and turning moral and intellectual energies of a rue order into the channel of ,elf-abnegating activity I It was a friendship that amply fulfilled the Promise of its initiatory rites. Through good and though ill report these blended Imes lived and laboured on; ceasing not to ! contribute to the slowly-tilling treasury of political wisdom, to- the growing fabric of ! righteous law end order, and to the life. giving currents of sweet human pity, social I purity, and international concord, It is not *say to write the ozclinary language of news- paper comment when one has a theme of such unusual moral strength, and even true grandeur. Campbell—we mean the author of "The Pleasures ef Memory "—heard the superb defence of Joseph Cierrald in his trial for sedition, before the Edinburgh Justi- ciary. and this refers to it, —" At this finish I was moved, and turning to a stranger beside me —apparently a tradesman-4 said to him, !By heavens, sir, that is a great man ! ' !Yes, air,' was the reply, 'he is not only great himself, but he makes every other man feel great who listens to him.' " Now, this is just how we feel about Mr. Bright's oratory and influence. He may not always carry our intellect with him to his precise conclusions in matters of detail, as, for in- stance, in some of the cases referred to in his resume of European conflicts. Even there, however, we feel that his standard is only too high tor men and nations in their at present crude and undeveloped condition. The world cannot grow in knowledge and charity unless the prophetic element assert itself prominently in our social and political life. Men and women must have ideals; and if they are "after the pattern shown in the mount "—ofa heavenly rather then of an earthly type—so much the better. We can buy tact and policy in any market, but wis- dom is more precious than rubies; and the weird spoken in season, out of a heart brim. ful of reverence for humanity even in its low estate, is more highly esteemed by the lover of men than a hollow rhetoric whose glittering crystals I only cover a cold and unsympathising heart. Therefore, we hail such utterances: as those of Mr. Bright at Bradford, They mean more than political manifestoes usually do. They have the ring of genuine patriotism ; and the lengthy and ripe ex- patience which they embody entitle them, I no lima than the accent of clear conviction which is everywhere present, to the respect and gratitude which genius devoted to the highest ends can alone inspire. Turning to the more practical side of our subject, we may note the signs of apprecia- tion, not merely of the characters, but of the public services of these twin brethren in the agitation for Corn Law Repeal. The statue unveilefi. at Bradford the other day and consecratd by such words of simple truth and nobleness, is the gift of • deceased tel American, Mr. J. H. Booth. It is said to I represent the exterior of the great Free Trader as fairly as marble could ever do. The crush of reporters for newspapers great and small wan an edifying sight. Truly, the eons adorn the sepulchres of those who cried long ere the fathers heard! The change in public opinion respecting com- mercial reciprocity is nearly complete. Cob- den's triumph was the triumph of reason over unreflecting obstinacy and selfishness. His method and manner were as simple as his aim. And, if it be a test of human character to have laid heart and life open to the gaze of a faithful and high-minded friend, then, in the worshipful affection which he inspired in the breast of Mr. Bright, we have collateral proof that his motives, like his acts and words were clear as noonday, and his domestic affections of a piece with his public services. It was a graceful thing for our American cousin to do; but Cobden's truest and most lasting monument is his plate in history, and in his countrymen's hearts.

AT the quarterly meeting of the Manches- ter Chamber of Commerce, held on Monday last, Mr. Edmund Ashworth, the president, made an interesting speech on the present condition of trade. As everyone knows, Mr. E. Ashworth is a sound political economist and tree-trader. Being a cotton manufac- turer himself, he knows what he is talking sb at, and he made mincemeat of Mr. Faw- cett in • few words, with regard to the Indian import duties. Mr. Ashworth said '' Shall the 200,000,000 of people in India continue to pay live per cent. more for their clothing in order that the mills of Bombay_may reap in additional rive per cent.? It really is lamentable at this time of day to offer any arguments in favour of protective duties. In the House of Com- mon,, on the 1102 ultimo, • resolution, pro- posed by Mr. Hugh Bircey, and seconded by Mr. Jacob Bright, in railed°, to the Indian Import duties upon cotton manufactures was agreed to without • division The subject wee diecureed in the most exhaustive fashion, I and the Lancashire members, including Mr. Birley. Mr. Jacob Bright, Mr. Briggs, Mr. , 0. 0. Welker, and Mr. Sidebotham, showed the utter fallacy and the gross injustice of the Indian import duties. The preteetive I duties actually burn the candle at both ends.] The wearer of the cello° pays more for his clothes, twenty as they are, than he ought I to do, and the Lancashire manufacturer pope I more for the produotion of his shirting. At the commencement of his address, Mr. Ashworth said " Trade I continued to hold out no prospect of early improvement ; in fact the Board of Trade returns for the eix months ' , ending Inns, 1877, showed a total decrease of £3,97t.000, when compared with the exports of the six months ending in June, 1878." But the ameunt of exports and imports for one quarter, or even one or two years, is really no reliable criterion of the prosperity or soundnees of trade. Ship- ments of goods are frequently much in ex- am of the real wants of the ports to whieh they are forwarded. A few weeks ago, there wail an interesting meeting of cotton mer- chants and brokers, held in Liverpool. The meeting included representatives of Ameri- can plantets, American cotton brokers, Lan oashire cotton spinners, Liverpool cotton dealers, and brokers, and other interested parties. During the discussion which oc- curred at that meeting one fact became very 'Tweet to us. It was this—that the sound- ness of the cotton trade was becoming very much deteriorated and undermined by no undue extension of the credit eyetem to the debate which took place in the Rouse of Commons on the Indian import duties, Mr. Jacob Bright, Mr. Walker, Mr. Briggs, and Mr. Sidebotham, all testified to the tact that taken es a whole, Lancashire cotton spinners end manufacturers were not • rich body. It is a painful fact that the cotton trade has been becoming poorer and poorer during the last twenty year.. Mr. Cobden pointed out the tendency when the American civil war broke out fifteen years BiLlOO. At the Liver- pool convention the credit system was dis- cussed, and several authorities were of opinion that the old system of paying cash down for raw cottru ought to be reverted to. Without wishing to lay down any hard and fast lines upon the subject, we must say that long credits either for the raw material or the manufactured product are prejudicial to trade. How can a capitalist who pays twenty shillings in the pound contend against I manufacturer who merely turns a lot of l machinery which he has never paid for, and Imakes bargains for so many bales of cotton which he has never seen, which really have no existence perhaps, but have to be pro- duced at some given time by hook or by crook. No one knows better than Mr. Ash- worth, who is • bona fide cotton spinner and ! capitalist, that the long credit system is the curse of the cotton trade, sod it is very right, just, and proper that it should be so. It is opposed to all the laws of political economy, ! that a person without means should be able to compete in trade with another who has money in his puree or at his bankers. ! Bankers have begun to find out the fallacy ! of owning mills and warehouses. So far, that is well. The next best thing is to etop I ! the supplies to agents. Cotton brokers. and! ! yarn and cloth agenta are a noceasity, and useful to both buyers and sellers, but when they become money lenders and pawn- broker,, they begin to sap the foundation. of trade, and are really the cause of much of the mischief which the Manchester Chamber of Commerce was cogitating upon on Mon- day. My mind's made up," and Bell and repent," where old phrases half a century ago, which actually became identified with individuals connected with Lancashire cotton

How can a man say that his mind's made up, or declare that he will sell and repent, when heir not his own master' I but in the hands of an agent or broker who hee to had him the means to pay his wages. The faster his money, or rather his agent's money goes, the more must his machinery go, and his task-master, the steam engine, I keeps inexorably driving on. It is the old I story, " You cannot make a silk purse out I of a sow's ear," and the sooner Lancashire cotton spoilers and manufacturers look at I their trade in that light the better.

In is some time since the Registrar-General has Mimed so unfavourable • report of the health of Altrincham as the one just issued en the health of the town and sub-districta during the second period of this year. The mortality shows a considerable increase, and the principal zymotic diseases were provident. Small pox especially figures largely, as in the last quarter this disease alone carried off 21. For the last few quarters it has been on the increase, for in December period it was only fatal in one case, then in March we had nine, and in the next and last quar- ter there were 21. 6peciM attention was called to the fact of the one death in Decem- ber, and if only common and ordinary pre- cautions had been used we should not now have to deplore the extent it has gained. This is not the only dreaded disease in Altrincham, for scarlet fever, though slightly on the decline, was fatal in three cases. There were also three deaths from fever. It will thus be seen that in the last quarter the town and sub-districts must have suffered greatly from these three diseases. If no im- provement is discernible in the current quar- ter, Altrincham will gain a notoriety which would prove hurtful to the interests of the town.

IF the Daily Telegraph's news from the seat of war may be accepted for once without these large reservations which those who prefer facts to vain imaginings are accustomed to make when that journal's war statements are under consideration, the Russian arms have just sustained a most serious reverse at ?loins, and its generally victorious progress decisively arrested. The newspaper in position announced on Wed- nesday that the result of the two days' battle had been the rout of the Russians, with a loss of 8,000 killed and 16,000 wounded. A telegram from a Russian source admits that in Tuesday's battle the Czar's troops were " unsucoesafal." Thin success may have an important influence on the fortunes of the campaign. With a strong Turkish force at i-levne and Mehemet Ali in unbroken strength at Rasgrad, the Russian Staff must feel much anxiety for the safety of their line of communications with General tiourko's force across the Balkans. the Roumanian army is crossing the Danube with the avowed purpose of menacing Osman Pasha's communications with Widin, and heavy Waken reinforcements are pouring into Roumania. There is n further news of importance from Armenia, but if the report of a renewed advance to the south- ward of Kars on the Erzeroum road should be confirmed, heavy fighing is in store for Mukhtar Pasha and his army, although from several quarters we hear that the season is too far advanced to permit ot the movements of large bodies of troops in the mountains of Armenia. Ever since the Turkish officials have made the—to them—astonishing discovery that their hideous barbarities in Bulgaria ; have actually lost to them a considerable • amount of sympathy in Europe and cease- Anent support, these acute persons have lAgue with extraordinary zeal, to reproach the RUNiani with similar cruelties, ap- patently in the hope that what has un- deniably weakened the arm of the Porte will do a like ills-service to their enemy. Indeed each side continues to accuse the other of horrible barbaiities. Colonel Wellesley has, it is said, addressed a report to Lord Derby denying that the Russian soldiers have committed the outrages imputed to them. The special correspondent of the Standard with the Russians gives a terrible account of the atrocities perpetrated by Oa. lurks en the Russian wounded, which he personally investigated on the spot. The narrative is of great value as embodying the teetimony of an English gentleman whose veracity cannot be called in question. The correspondent comes to the conclusion that the Turks are "a, savage Is the Aahantees," of whose barbarous conduct he was a witness on the march to Coomaseie. The oredence which one would properly I refuse to the Telegraph must be accorded to the Daily Deice, a paper whose reports from ! the first have been remarkable tor their rarely-challenged accuracy. This journal !says—." No doubt that the Russian forces operating against Osman Pacha have sus- tained every severe defeat, the consequences of which it would be rash to predict. The 1:11111e is not like that of General Schilder- flohuldner's repulse ten days ago at the same place. The Russian attack on Monday last was planned after the warning afforded by that reverse. The Russian commander knew the conditions which he had to satisfy ; he has failed to meet them, and his soldiers, who never fought more bravely, have had to pay the penalty." The Daily News adds " The Turks have at length come to under- stand that Europe regards their rule as in- tolerable, and that it must be modified as it only can be by foreign interference. For four hundred years the Ottoman Turks have believed that the power to conquer conclu- sively established the right to rule the oonquered, as they understand ruling, and have despised the humane art of govern- ment. It stirs their blood to find that their brutal and brutalising domination has been condemned by all Europe, and that in the war which it has justified, and by which it will be either overthrown or abated, they ! have no allies. But the vices and crimes which have made the Ottoman Government a scandal and a nuisance are those of the governing classes, and all travellers draw • broad distinction between them and the common Moslem population whioh have to defend their superiors in the field whenever ! the power of the latter is threatened. The Turkish private soldier is brave, for he ! has been taught that, poor, ragged, and un- shed as he may be, he belongs to a superior race. He is patient, obedient, and holds his life always at the disposal of his commander. We have never been among those, if there are such, who are mild to underrate Turkish ! valour, any more than we have been able to admit that every virtue and high qualifies- ! don for government is summed up in cour- age. We have not the least doubt that the Turks will fight well in this war, and that they will make those opposed to them pay dear for the victory which sooner or later is likely to be theirs."
